findings.title: AppliedArtworkStore.GetAsync reads the shared cache without the lock that guards its writer

findings.locality_impact: The hazard is contained to this one Module; fixing it here fixes every caller at once.

builder_notes.pattern: Churn concentrates where concerns are merged
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: One file dominates the six-month edit count and is several times larger than everything else; commits touching it describe unrelated changes (a ranking tweak, a UI fix, a parsing fix) in the same file.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: When a file's edit count and size both dominate the repo, treat that as a leaky-seam signal before writing the next feature into it - extract the concern that changed, don't add to the pile.
builder_notes.stack_example: C#/UWP: a Page code-behind file is a natural dumping ground because event handlers must live there; pure business logic (ranking, parsing, name resolution) does not have to - move it to a plain static class or service the Page calls into.

builder_notes.pattern: A lock that guards the writer but not the reader is not a lock
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: A SemaphoreSlim (or lock) wraps every write to a shared mutable collection, but at least one read path skips it because 'it's just a read.'
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Every access path to lock-protected shared mutable state takes the same lock, reads included - a Dictionary read racing a Dictionary write is exactly as unsafe as two racing writes.
builder_notes.stack_example: C#: Dictionary<K,V> is not thread-safe for any concurrent read+write mix; either guard every access uniformly or switch to ConcurrentDictionary<K,V>.

builder_notes.pattern: Sequential await in a per-item loop hides its own cost until the collection grows
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: A foreach loop with an await inside it, over items whose network/IO calls don't depend on each other, and no Task.WhenAll / bounded-parallel pattern anywhere nearby.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Before parallelizing, check what the loop body writes to outside itself (caches, counters) - if those aren't thread-safe, fix that first or the 'optimization' introduces the very race the sequential version was accidentally protecting against.
builder_notes.stack_example: C#: Task.WhenAll over a bounded batch (via SemaphoreSlim) turns N sequential round-trips into N/batch-size overlapped ones, but only after any shared Dictionary the bodies write to becomes a ConcurrentDictionary.

findings.title: LoadGameEntriesAsync's manifest parser bypassed JsonRead at five call sites, so one JSON-null field silently dropped the rest of that folder's games
findings.why_it_matters: The widget's primary load path could silently hide an entire platform folder's worth of games from the user with no visible error, whenever any single manifest entry had one of five commonly-nullable fields explicitly JSON null.
findings.what_is_wrong: LoadGameEntriesAsync read five manifest fields (id, addedDate, imagePath, title, installLocation/executableName) with the raw Windows.Data.Json accessors (GetNamedString, ContainsKey) instead of the codebase's own JsonRead module, which exists specifically to tolerate a member that is present and JSON null. Empirically confirmed this loop (new test in SteamGridDB.Xbox.Tests/JsonReadTests.cs): GetNamedString(name) and GetNamedString(name, default) both throw InvalidOperationException when the named member is present and JSON null, and ContainsKey(name) returns true for that same null-valued member - so the ContainsKey("id") guard at the top of the entry loop did not protect against a null id. None of the five raw accesses sat inside a per-entry try/catch; the nearest one is the per-folder try/catch several stack frames up, wrapping the entire gameCache walk. A single manifest entry with one null field therefore threw past every sibling entry still to be processed in that folder, silently aborting the rest of the folder's parse (Debug.WriteLine only, invisible outside an attached debugger) instead of just skipping the one malformed entry. JsonRead.cs's own docstring documents this exact failure class already shipping once in this codebase, on a different call site (SteamGridDbClient's Steam app ID field) - the fix that produced JsonRead was never carried into the manifest loader, the largest and most-churned file in the repo.

builder_notes.pattern: A carried-forward backlog item's proposed remedy can be correct even when a related, differently-scoped remedy failed the same test - don't let a prior failed attempt poison a genuinely narrower reframing of the same finding.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: A backlog item explicitly framed as "the corrected, narrower version of X" after X failed the Simplify Pressure Test - the narrower version deserves its own fresh SPT pass, not inherited rejection.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Before rejecting a queued remedy because "something like this failed before," re-read the queued remedy's actual scope and re-run SPT on that scope specifically, not the scope of the prior failed attempt.

builder_notes.pattern: A pure computation buried inside a large orchestration method can be verified fully separable by checking data dependencies in both directions - not just whether later code needs it, but whether the code it sits next to needs anything it produces.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: An inline block bracketed by side-effecting code (I/O calls, continue statements, mutable counters) on either side - check whether the block's inputs are all available before the surrounding code runs, and whether its outputs are needed by nothing until after.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Trace every local variable the candidate block reads and writes; if none of its reads come from the surrounding side-effecting code and none of its writes feed back into it, the block is safe to extract without reordering.

builder_notes.pattern: A theoretically-racy static mutable cache is not evidence of a live concurrency defect if nothing in the codebase actually calls it from more than one execution path.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: Unlocked static Dictionary writes with a check-then-fetch-then-write shape - before flagging as a finding, grep the whole codebase for Task.WhenAll, Parallel.*, Task.Run, and any other concurrent-dispatch mechanism; if none exists and every caller is reached through a single sequential loop, the hazard is latent, not live.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: A concurrency finding needs two things, not one - an unsynchronized shared write AND a source-verified concurrent call path. Missing the second downgrades it to a landmine note on whichever finding would introduce the concurrent path.

builder_notes.pattern: When a proposed seam's second adapter would have to be a hand-built fake simulating an external system, check first whether the decision logic that actually needs testing is separable from the fetch. Async functions that call the network often already reduce their inputs to plain values before deciding what to do with them - extracting from that point needs no seam, no fake, and no new mutable state at all.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: A Finding's why it matters names one specific comparison/boundary as the risk, not the whole untested function - that's a signal the decision, not the fetch, is what actually needs coverage.
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Before proposing any seam, find where the function already reduces its network/IO result to plain values, and extract from that point forward as a pure static method.
builder_notes.stack_example: C# - ArtworkDownloader.FindOfficialLookalikeAsync already computed candidateMatch/candidateLayout as doubles before deciding; PassesColourAndLayoutGate(double, double, double) needed neither a Fetcher delegate nor a mock HTTP client.

builder_notes.pattern: A settable static delegate (Func<T>) proposed as a test seam for a true-external dependency is architecturally different from a settable static property proposed for a local-substitutable one, even though both look like the same idiom on the surface - the file-system case swaps between two real adapters, the network case would swap a real call for fabricated data.
builder_notes.how_to_recognize: Before reusing an existing settable-static-property idiom for a new seam, check the Dependency Categorization of what's being swapped - local-substitutable (real thing, different location/instance) vs true-external (real remote system; the test side would have to be fabricated).
builder_notes.smallest_coding_rule: Only reuse the settable-static idiom directly when the test-side value can be a REAL instance of the same type; when the test side would have to be hand-fabricated data pretending to be a response, treat it as a new architectural decision needing its own two-adapter analysis.
